newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Brittan-EU backs telecom pact despite US exemption.
newsitem.headline: Brittan-EU backs telecom pact despite US exemption.

text.p: EU Trade Representative Sir Leon Brittan said that ministers from the 13-member body on Friday endorsed a global telecom accord despite a U.S. exemption on satellite transmission services which the EU termed "illegal."

Brittan, speaking to reporters after the late-night ministerial meeting, also said that the EU had been assured by U.S. officials that the Most-Favoured-Nation (MFN) exemption would not be used against EU member states.
"The EU has decided to go along with the agreement... We regret the U.S. has taken an MFN exemption," Brittan said.
"We regard it (the U.S. exemption) as a negative step but we don't regard it as a deal-breaker, although we consider it illegal," he added.
"We have been told by the U.S. that the U.S. exemption will not be applied against the EU," Brittan said.
He declined to say whether such assurances had been given in a telephone call with Acting U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky, who is in Washington.
"We regard the exception as illegal and reserve any rights in that respect," Brittan added. "We have stated it is illegal to prevent it setting a precedent in other negotiations."

The U.S. exemption to Most-Favoured-Nation treatment for direct-to-home broadcast and direct broadcast satellite television services as well as digital audiovisual services was presented at telecom talks at the World Trade Organisation.
The U.S. restrictions were primarily aimed at Canada whose own offer was strongly criticised by Washington, diplomats said.
Sixty-seven governments have presented offers to liberalise the $800 billion a year industry by opening their markets to foreign operators. They are due to seal the deal on Saturday.
"We have a good possibility of success," U.S. Deputy Trade Representative Jeffrey Lang, told reporters earlier.
Brittan said: "The agreement as a whole is a huge success for the WTO. We feel the benefits to world trade will be enormous, some $600 billion will be opened up."
"We have to finalise the deal tomorrow, cross the t's and dot the i's," he added.

"The EU has confirmed its offer. We are glad that after the reluctance of last year, the U.S. has been persuaded to join the club," Brittan said, referring to Washington's backing away from a deal last April saying other offers were insufficient. (( - Stephanie Nebehay, Reuters Geneva Newsroom 41-22-733 38 31))
